proof:
# Exact failure of a heavy-face / heavy-affine-piece induction

Take n=2,d=1 and P=conv{(0,0),(2,0),(0,2)}. Its lattice points consist of its three vertices

V={(0,0),(2,0),(0,2)}

and its three edge midpoints

E={(1,0),(0,1),(1,1)}.

Thus P has no interior lattice point and has lattice width two. For the latter assertion, a nonzero integer normal (a,b) takes values 0,2a,2b at the vertices, whose range is at least two; the normal (1,0) attains range two.

Let C in R^2 x R be the convex hull of

union_{v in V} ({v} x [-1/5,1/5])

and

union_{e in E} ({e} x [-1/2,1/2]).

This is a full-dimensional convex body: it contains P x [-1/5,1/5]. Its projection is exactly P, so there are only the six listed nonempty integer fibers.

At a vertex v of P, any convex combination projecting to v uses only points over v, so the fiber is exactly [-1/5,1/5]. At an edge midpoint e, the supporting line of that edge forces any convex combination projecting to e to use only points over that edge. These have continuous coordinates in [-1/2,1/2], while the entire interval [-1/2,1/2] over e was inserted in the generating set. Hence that fiber is exactly [-1/2,1/2].

Therefore the three vertex fibers have volume 2/5 each, the three midpoint fibers have volume one each, and total mixed volume is

M=3(2/5)+3=21/5.

The largest single fiber has mass one, strictly below M/4=21/20. Thus the heavy-fiber lemma does not apply.

Every line in the integer-coordinate plane contains at most mass two from these six fibers. To check this, the only lines containing three of the six base points are the three boundary edge lines, whose masses are 2/5+1+2/5=9/5. Every other line contains at most two points, each of mass at most one; the bound two is attained by lines through two distinct edge midpoints. The three midpoints are noncollinear.

Consequently every rank-one affine piece has mass at most two, strictly below M/2=21/10; every rank-zero affine piece has mass at most one, strictly below M/4=21/20.

Applying the conjectural (r,d) induction bound to a rank-r affine piece gives gamma_d*mass(piece)/2^r. For both r=0 and r=1, this certified quantity is at most gamma_d, strictly below the desired gamma_d*M/4=(21/20)gamma_d. Thus no selection of a proper affine piece, even one that is not a face, has sufficient mass for a one-piece dimension-reduction proof.

This example also rules out a cover of these six weighted fibers by proper affine pieces with total cost sum_i 2^{r_i}<=4. Indeed the mass of each rank-r piece is at most 2^r, so such a cover would give M<=sum_i mass(piece_i)<=4, contradicting M=21/5. The conclusion holds even if the cover overlaps. Fractional covers with nonnegative coefficients and coverage at least one are similarly impossible with total weighted cost at most four, by multiplying each bound by its coefficient and summing.

This is not a counterexample to OC. It demonstrates that lattice-free projection plus lower-rank induction does not yield the exact constant through a universal heavy-face or affine-piece-cover budget.

## A variant with nonaffine fiber centroids

The obstruction is not dependent on an affine centroid map. Keep the vertex intervals [-1/5,1/5], but give the unit-length midpoint fibers at (1,0),(0,1),(1,1) respective centers 1/4,-1/4,0. Thus their intervals are [-1/4,3/4],[-3/4,1/4],[-1/2,1/2]. Form the convex hull of these six fiber segments.

The projection and exact vertex fibers are unchanged. At a fixed edge midpoint, every convex combination projecting to that midpoint is a mixture of its prescribed interval and the average of its two endpoint intervals; the latter is [-1/5,1/5]. This interval is contained in each prescribed midpoint interval. Therefore each midpoint fiber also remains exactly the specified unit interval. All weights and all preceding bounds are unchanged.

An affine function on the base triangle that agrees with the three vertex centroids must be identically zero. It cannot equal the centroids 1/4 and -1/4 at the two specified edge midpoints. Thus this variant has a nonaffine fiber-centroid map.
